You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions (English (en)). The languages are equal peers; none is the original. One or more of them may have changed since Swedish was last brought up to date. You have the current page of each other language and the current Swedish page. You have no diff and no earlier version, so you cannot see what changed: only how the pages compare as they are now.

Your job is to bring the Swedish page up to date with the current English page: find what it says that Swedish does not, or says differently, and make the edits a careful editor of the Swedish page would make so that it says the same things.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Many differences between the pages are deliberate, not changes waiting to be made. Keep all of that. It follows that:
- A fact that differs may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish states it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A difference may need no edit at all: when Swedish says the same thing in its own words, or leaves something out or adds something on purpose.
- A difference in order or structure is not a reason to reorder Swedish.
- Something that only looks like a difference, but says the same thing, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: every place where the Swedish page no longer says what the other pages say, quoted from both, with whether you think it is a change waiting to be made in Swedish or a difference on purpose, and why.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

Your job is not to translate the diff. Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Markup is not text. You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Your job is to bring the Swedish page up to date with the current English page: find what it says that Swedish does not, or says differently, and make the edits a careful editor of the Swedish page would make so that it says the same things.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:

Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Markup is not text. You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions (English (en)). The languages are equal peers; none is the original. One or more of them may have changed since Swedish was last brought up to date. You have the current page of each other language and the current Swedish page. You have no diff and no earlier version, so you cannot see what changed: only how the pages compare as they are now.

Your job is to bring the Swedish page up to date with the current English page: find what it says that Swedish does not, or says differently, and make the edits a careful editor of the Swedish page would make so that it says the same things.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Many differences between the pages are deliberate, not changes waiting to be made. Keep all of that. It follows that:
- A fact that differs may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish states it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A difference may need no edit at all: when Swedish says the same thing in its own words, or leaves something out or adds something on purpose.
- A difference in order or structure is not a reason to reorder Swedish.
- Something that only looks like a difference, but says the same thing, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: every place where the Swedish page no longer says what the other pages say, quoted from both, with whether you think it is a change waiting to be made in Swedish or a difference on purpose, and why.

Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have the content from when English was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have the content from when English was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have the content from when English was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

Your job is to bring the English page up to date with the current Swedish page: find what it says that English does not, or says differently, and make the edits a careful editor of the English page would make so that it says the same things.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions (Swedish (sv)). The languages are equal peers; none is the original. One or more of them may have changed since English was last brought up to date. You have the current page of each other language and the current English page. You have no diff and no earlier version, so you cannot see what changed: only how the pages compare as they are now.

Your job is to bring the English page up to date with the current Swedish page: find what it says that English does not, or says differently, and make the edits a careful editor of the English page would make so that it says the same things.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Many differences between the pages are deliberate, not changes waiting to be made. Keep all of that. It follows that:
- A fact that differs may need several edits in English: everywhere English states it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A difference may need no edit at all: when English says the same thing in its own words, or leaves something out or adds something on purpose.
- A difference in order or structure is not a reason to reorder English.
- Something that only looks like a difference, but says the same thing, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: every place where the English page no longer says what the other pages say, quoted from both, with whether you think it is a change waiting to be made in English or a difference on purpose, and why.

Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have the content from when English was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have the content from when English was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since English was last brought up to date, someone changed Swedish (sv). For each language that changed, you have the content from when English was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the English version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in English: everywhere English says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when English does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where English follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the English file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

One or more of them may have changed since English was last brought up to date. You have the current page of each other language and the current English page. You have no diff and no earlier version, so you cannot see what changed: only how the pages compare as they are now.

Your job is to bring the English page up to date with the current Swedish page: find what it says that English does not, or says differently, and make the edits a careful editor of the English page would make so that it says the same things.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Many differences between the pages are deliberate, not changes waiting to be made. Keep all of that. It follows that:

- A difference in order or structure is not a reason to reorder English.
- Something that only looks like a difference, but says the same thing, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions (Swedish (sv)). The languages are equal peers; none is the original. One or more of them may have changed since English was last brought up to date. You have the current page of each other language and the current English page. You have no diff and no earlier version, so you cannot see what changed: only how the pages compare as they are now.

Your job is to bring the English page up to date with the current Swedish page: find what it says that English does not, or says differently, and make the edits a careful editor of the English page would make so that it says the same things.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Many differences between the pages are deliberate, not changes waiting to be made. Keep all of that. It follows that:
- A fact that differs may need several edits in English: everywhere English states it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A difference may need no edit at all: when English says the same thing in its own words, or leaves something out or adds something on purpose.
- A difference in order or structure is not a reason to reorder English.
- Something that only looks like a difference, but says the same thing, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: every place where the English page no longer says what the other pages say, quoted from both, with whether you think it is a change waiting to be made in English or a difference on purpose, and why.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You are keeping the English (en) version of a document up to date with its other language versions (Swedish (sv)). The languages are equal peers; none is the original. One or more of them may have changed since English was last brought up to date. You have the current page of each other language and the current English page. You have no diff and no earlier version, so you cannot see what changed: only how the pages compare as they are now.

Your job is to bring the English page up to date with the current Swedish page: find what it says that English does not, or says differently, and make the edits a careful editor of the English page would make so that it says the same things.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Many differences between the pages are deliberate, not changes waiting to be made. Keep all of that. It follows that:
- A fact that differs may need several edits in English: everywhere English states it, so that English does not contradict itself.
- A difference may need no edit at all: when English says the same thing in its own words, or leaves something out or adds something on purpose.
- A difference in order or structure is not a reason to reorder English.
- Something that only looks like a difference, but says the same thing, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for English. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose English pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in English follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is English, written as a English writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: every place where the English page no longer says what the other pages say, quoted from both, with whether you think it is a change waiting to be made in English or a difference on purpose, and why.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the English file. Each edit's result shows the English file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the English file, fix it with further edits. When the English file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Your job is to bring the Swedish page up to date with the current English page: find what it says that Swedish does not, or says differently, and make the edits a careful editor of the Swedish page would make so that it says the same things.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Many differences between the pages are deliberate, not changes waiting to be made. Keep all of that. It follows that:

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

  ctaLink="/sv/missa-inte/"
  backgroundMedia="/media/start-video-002-optimized.mp4"
  poster="/media/home/hero-poster.jpg"
/>

<CmSection id="sect-e5f6a7b8"
  heading="Vad är Acme?"
  contain="true"
  align="left"
  body={"Acme hjälper dig som arrangerar turneringar att enkelt och smidigt ge en fantastisk helhetsupplevelse till dina deltagare. Från anmälning, betallösning, lottning och spelschema till liverapportering av mål och slutresultat till webb, mobilappar eller sms.\n\nVi har gjort det enkelt för stora, små, enkla och komplexa turneringar."}
  divider={true}
  contained={true}
/>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-4a6e82d1"
  eyebrow="ENKLA BETALLÖSNINGAR"
  title="Ta enkelt betalt med kort, Klarna eller Swish"
  ctaText="Läs mer om vår betallösning"
  ctaLink="/sv/kort-och-klarna/"
  image="/media/home/klarna_acme-3.webp"
  imageAlt="Betalning med Klarna i Acme"
  imagePosition="right"
  bgColor="light"
  imageFocus="left center"
>
  Med vår moderna betallösning kan ni slippa alla bankbetalningar. Låt lagen betala med kort eller Klarna vilket gör att betalningarna registreras automatiskt i systemet och ni får era pengar direkt.
</CmFeatureRow>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-2c8d91e4"
  eyebrow="Smartare schemaläggning med AI"
  title="Så fungerar det i Acme"
  ctaText="Läs mer om AI i Acme här"
  ctaLink="/sv/vara-ai-losningar/"
  image="/media/home/ai-image-copy-1.webp"
  imageAlt="AI-schemaläggning i Acme"
  imagePosition="left"
  bgColor="white"
>
  Att lägga ett fungerande spelschema är ett komplext pussel – särskilt när det handlar om hundratals eller tusentals matcher, flera spelplatser, vilotider och specialönskemål.
</CmFeatureRow>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-91d5c0e7"
  eyebrow="VI ÄR STOLTA ÖVER VÅR SUPPORT"
  title="Support i världsklass"
  ctaText="Läs mer om vår support här"
  ctaLink="/sv/support/"
  image="/media/home/support.webp"
  imageAlt="Acme-supporten"
  imagePosition="left"
  bgColor="white"
>
  Den kanske mest definierande delen av Acme är vår support. Vi arbetar hårt för att alla i företaget har som yttersta mål att hjälpa våra kunder. Vi finns tillgängliga varje dag för att hjälpa er med allt från enskilda frågor till att assistera med spelschema och rådgivning. Vi svarar på svenska, norska och engelska.
</CmFeatureRow>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-5b0e7a13"
  eyebrow="LIVESTREAMING MED GLOBEX LIVE"
  title="Sänd alla matcher live – och tjäna pengar på det"
  ctaText="Läs mer om livestreaming"
  ctaLink="/sv/streaming/"
  image="/media/streaming/pix4team-camera.gif"
  imageAlt="AI-kamera på stativ som automatiskt följer matchen"
  imagePosition="right"
  bgColor="light"
>
  Tillsammans med vår partner Globex Live kan ni livestreama alla matcher med AI-kameror som följer spelet automatiskt. Tittarna betalar per match eller för hela turneringen – en ny intäktskälla för cupen.
</CmFeatureRow>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-c3b90f52"
  eyebrow="ENGAGERA ERA BESÖKARE"
  title="Er egen mobilapp för Android och iPhone"
  ctaText="Skaffa en app för er turnering"
  ctaLink="/sv/app/"
  image="/media/home/usp-mobile-app.jpg"
  imageAlt="Egen mobilapp för turneringen"
  imagePosition="left"
  bgColor="white"
>
  Vi kan hjälpa er att få er egen mobilapp för turneringen. Vi gör allt arbete med att utveckla appen och den blir sedan kopplad till turneringen i Acme vilket gör att ni kan administrera allt från ett och samma ställe.
</CmFeatureRow>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-7f04b3a9"
  eyebrow="CASE STUDIE: FJORDBY BASKET FESTIVAL"
  title="En av våra kunder berättar"
  ctaText="Läs om Fjordby Basket Festival här"
  ctaLink="/sv/fjordby-basket-festival/"
  image="/media/home/customer-story.png"
  imageAlt="Fjordby Basket Festival"
  imagePosition="right"
  bgColor="light"
>
  Läs vårt reportage om en lyckad resa för basket och Fjordby i Norge. Ola Nordvik berättar lite om deras resa, hur de avancerat, lyckats och fortsätter att sätta upp nya mål i framtiden med sin turnering.
</CmFeatureRow>

<CmBandHeading id="band-5e17d8f0"
  heading="Mer information för den intresserade"
  bg="white"
  align="left"
  contained={true}
/>

<CmColumns id="cols-8b2f47c6"
  align="left"
  columns="2"
  gap="48"
  maxWidth={1140}
>
  <CmColumn id="col-d94a10e3"
    heading="Viktiga funktioner"
  >
    <TextBlock id="text-6c58e2b7">
      Missa inte att vi också har häftiga funktioner som livestreaming med Globex Live, liveresultat, egen hemsida för turneringen, boende & mat, domare, SMS-utskick och incheckning.
    </TextBlock>
    <CmButton id="btn-31f7a9d0"
      label="Läs mer om våra funktioner"
      href="/sv/missa-inte/"
      variant="green"
      icon="none"
    />
  </CmColumn>
  <CmColumn id="col-59a3e8d7"
    heading="Prissättning"
  >
    <TextBlock id="text-c21f80b4">
      Vi har en enkel prissättning som passar både små och stora turneringar i olika sporter. Förutom en lagbaserad licens finns det många extratjänster att välja till!
    </TextBlock>
    <CmButton id="btn-e40b97c3"
      label="Läs mer om våra priser"
      href="/sv/priser/"
      variant="green"
      icon="none"
    />
  </CmColumn>
</CmColumns>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-06c9e3b8"
  eyebrow="TA BETALT FÖR FÖRENINGEN"
  title="Acme Clubs"
  ctaText="Läs mer om Acme Clubs"
  ctaLink="https://clubs.acme.example/"
  image="/media/home/si.jpg"
  imageAlt="Acme Clubs"
  imagePosition="right"
  bgColor="light"
>
  Vår systerprodukt Acme Clubs används av uppemot 1000 klubbar för att samla in träningsavgifter och medlemsavgifter, i både Norge och Sverige. Systemet låter dig anpassa er insamling samtidigt som det är väldigt lättanvänt.
</CmFeatureRow>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-f15b72a0"
  eyebrow="IDROTT ÄR VIKTIGT I EN GLOBAL VÄRLD"
  title="Gemenskap, hopp och utveckling – både här hemma och i Östafrika."
  ctaText="Läs mer om samarbetet"
  ctaLink="/sv/lakeside-youth-cup/"
  image="/media/home/LakesideYouthCup.webp"
  imageAlt="Lakeside Youth Cup"
  imagePosition="left"
  bgColor="light"
>
  Vi samarbetar med Lakeside Youth Cup (LYC), en årlig ungdomsfestival i Tanzania som stärker unga genom idrott, utbildning och samhällsengagemang.
</CmFeatureRow>

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) version of a document up to date with its other language versions. The languages are equal peers; none is the original. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed English (en). For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

One or more of them may have changed since Swedish was last brought up to date. You have the current page of each other language and the current Swedish page. You have no diff and no earlier version, so you cannot see what changed: only how the pages compare as they are now.

Your job is to bring the Swedish page up to date with the current English page: find what it says that Swedish does not, or says differently, and make the edits a careful editor of the Swedish page would make so that it says the same things.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Many differences between the pages are deliberate, not changes waiting to be made. Keep all of that. It follows that:
- A fact that differs may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish states it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A difference may need no edit at all: when Swedish says the same thing in its own words, or leaves something out or adds something on purpose.
- A difference in order or structure is not a reason to reorder Swedish.
- Something that only looks like a difference, but says the same thing, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. One or more of them may have changed since Swedish was last brought up to date. You have the current page of each other language and the current Swedish page. You have no diff and no earlier version, so you cannot see what changed: only how the pages compare as they are now.

Your job is to bring the Swedish page up to date with the current English page: find what it says that Swedish does not, or says differently, and make the edits a careful editor of the Swedish page would make so that it says the same things.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Many differences between the pages are deliberate, not changes waiting to be made. Keep all of that. It follows that:
- A fact that differs may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish states it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A difference may need no edit at all: when Swedish says the same thing in its own words, or leaves something out or adds something on purpose.
- A difference in order or structure is not a reason to reorder Swedish.
- Something that only looks like a difference, but says the same thing, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: every place where the Swedish page no longer says what the other pages say, quoted from both, with whether you think it is a change waiting to be made in Swedish or a difference on purpose, and why.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.
